# Frame Inventory — Exercise Instructions

## 1. Scenario

In the **out-of-home (OOH) media** industry, advertisers buy time on physical
display surfaces such as roadside billboards, transport platforms, mall
screens, and bus shelters. Each surface is referred to as a **frame**, and an
operator's catalogue of frames — including their location, size, format,
status, and commercial attributes — is collectively known as the **frame
inventory**. Keeping that inventory accurate matters: every downstream process
(planning, pricing, booking, reporting) depends on it.

For this exercise the candidate will build a small but realistic service for
managing OOH frame inventory. Scoping is part of the exercise: the candidate
is not expected to deliver every feature one could imagine, but to pick a
meaningful subset and deliver it well.

## 2. What we provide

This repository is the starting point. It is intentionally minimal so the
candidate can make their own architectural choices, but it includes enough
infrastructure to skip the boilerplate and start delivering business value
straight away.

| Path                  | Contents                                                                          |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/backend/`        | Bare Spring Boot 3.5 + Java 21 module (Gradle). Exposes only `/api/health`.       |
| `src/frontend/`       | Next.js + React 19 + TypeScript module that calls the backend `/api/health` on boot. |
| `docker-compose.yml`  | One-command infra: backend, frontend, MongoDB, Postgres, OpenSearch + Dashboards.  |
| `data/`               | Extract from the legacy system — `inventory_frame.csv` (~1.3k OOH frame rows).    |
| `design-system/`      | Design system the frontend must be built against — components, tokens, guidance.  |
| `README.md`           | How to run the stack locally, ports, and credentials for the bundled services.    |

> **A note on the suggested infrastructure.** The `docker-compose.yml` file
> is a starting point, not a requirement. The candidate is free to swap any
> of these services for tooling they prefer (a different database, search
> engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final stack
> still runs end-to-end with a single command. If the candidate does choose
> to use the services provided here, they should pick **one** of the two
> datastores for their domain data — either `mongodb` *or* `postgres`,
> not both — and remove the service they don't need (along with its volume)
> so the stack reflects the design actually built.

In addition, the candidate receives:

- A **provisioned OpenAI Codex API key**. Use of an AI coding assistant is
  explicitly expected — we want to see how the candidate collaborates with a
  model, not whether they can hand-write every line.

## 3. Features

The candidate should deliver the following features:

1. **Add a frame.** A user can create a new frame through the application and
   see it persisted in the inventory.
2. **Edit a frame.** A user can amend an existing frame's attributes and have
   the changes saved.
3. **Bulk upload frames from a CSV.** A user can upload a CSV through the
   application and have the rows ingested into the inventory. The supplied
   `data/inventory_frame.csv` is the file to validate this feature
   against. This is a user-driven feature of the running app, not a one-off
   bootstrap step.
4. **View a frame's history.** A user can see the audit trail of changes to
   any given frame.

How these features are surfaced, structured, and tested is left to the
candidate's judgement.

## 4. Domain data

The shape of a frame is anchored by the legacy export shipped at
`data/inventory_frame.csv` (~1,300 rows) and by the prototype in
`design-system/`. The candidate is expected to inspect both and design a
domain model they are comfortable defending.

At a high level, each frame in the export carries:

- **Identity** — a frame identifier, plus references to downstream systems
  (Broadsign, pricing, linked frames).
- **Location** — country, region, town, postcode, latitude/longitude,
  address, and distance to the nearest school.
- **Site & position** — the kind of place the frame lives in (station,
  underground, roadside, airport, etc.) and where on that site it sits.
- **Format** — classic vs digital, format code, dimensions / pixels /
  aspect ratio, illumination, number of slots, size grouping.
- **Lifecycle** — created/modified timestamps, status, and a status reason.
- **Commercials** — impact weight, pricing grade, production rate card,
  premium flag.

The legacy column names and groupings are not prescriptive — the candidate
should design the domain model that best fits the features in §3, and
document the assumptions they made along the way.

## 5. Additional Requirements

Install and use the **[Entire CLI](https://entire.io)**. Entire hooks into the
candidate's git workflow and, on every push, captures the Codex agent
sessions that produced the changes and links them to the corresponding
commits as *checkpoints*. The result is a searchable record of how the
solution was actually built: the prompts used, the iterations the candidate
went through, the suggestions they accepted, and — just as important — the
ones they rejected or refined.

This is not about surveillance; it is about giving us a fair signal of
**how** the candidate works with AI tooling. We are far less interested in
whether code came from a human keystroke or a model completion than in
whether the candidate exercised judgement, scoped well, and reviewed the
output critically.

> **Note:** Codex support in Entire is currently in preview. The candidate
> should follow Entire's setup documentation for the latest supported
> workflow.

## 6. Submission

When the candidate is ready, they should share a **public GitHub repository**
containing their solution. The repository must include:

- All source code and anything else required to run the solution.
- A README explaining how to run it, the design decisions taken, and the
  trade-offs made.
- The Entire **checkpoints branch** with the captured Codex sessions linked
  to commits, so we can review the AI collaboration alongside the code.

There is no fixed deadline; we recommend timeboxing the exercise to a few
focused sessions rather than open-ended work. If something blocks progress,
note it in the README rather than over-investing time on it.
# AGENTS.md - Java Spring Boot & gRPC Development Guidelines

Behavioral and architectural guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes while strictly enforcing **SOLID principles**, Spring Boot + gRPC best practices, and clean code standards.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

## 1. Think Before Coding

**Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.**

Before implementing:

* State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.
* If multiple interpretations exist, present them — don't pick silently.
* If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.
* If something is unclear (e.g., `.proto` contract changes, transaction boundaries, or domain invariants), stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

## 2. Simplicity First

**Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.**

* No features or RPC endpoints beyond what was asked.
* No abstractions or Strategy interfaces for single-use code (apply OCP when variation actually exists or is requested).
* No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.
* No defensive `try-catch` blocks or error handling for impossible scenarios.
* If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

## 3. Surgical Changes

**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:

* Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
* Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
* Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
* If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it — don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

* Remove imports, variables, fields, or private methods that YOUR changes made unused.
* Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

* "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
* "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
* "Refactor X" → "Ensure unit and gRPC integration tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
[Step] → verify: [check]
[Step] → verify: [check]

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

## 5. Tech Stack & Conventions

* **Language:** Java 21+ (Prefer `record` for immutable domain DTOs/commands, pattern matching, and modern standard library features).
* **Framework:** Spring Boot 3.4+ with **Spring gRPC** (`org.springframework.grpc:spring-grpc-spring-boot-starter`).
* **Serialization / RPC:** Protocol Buffers (`proto3`) & gRPC.
* **Build Tool:** Maven or Gradle (Respect existing project configuration and `protobuf` compiler plugins).
* **Dependency Injection:** **ALWAYS** use Constructor Injection. Field injection (`@Autowired` on fields) is strictly forbidden.
* **Null Safety:** Avoid returning `null` from methods. Use `Optional<T>` for repository/service lookups that may not yield a result, and use `@NonNull` / `@Nullable` annotations where appropriate.

## 6. Build, Protobuf & Test Commands

Use these standard commands to compile Protobuf definitions and verify changes:

* **Maven:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./mvnw protobuf:compile protobuf:compile-custom`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./mvnw test`
  * Run a single test class: `./mvnw test -Dtest=ClassName`
* **Gradle:**
  * Compile Protobuf stubs: `./gradlew generateProto`
  * Run unit & integration tests: `./gradlew test`
  * Run a single test class: `./gradlew test --tests "*ClassName"`

## 7. SOLID Principles in Spring Boot & gRPC

### S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

*A class should have one, and only one, reason to change.*

* **gRPC Adapters (`*ImplBase` subclasses) & Controllers:** Responsible *only* for handling transport concerns—unwrapping and validating incoming Protobuf messages (or HTTP requests), delegating to an application service/use case, mapping the domain result back to a Protobuf response, and completing the `StreamObserver` (`onNext()` / `onCompleted()`). Never put business logic or direct repository calls in a gRPC service implementation.
* **Services (`@Service`):** Contain pure business logic and transaction boundaries (`@Transactional`). Break down large "God Services" into smaller, cohesive, domain-focused services or use cases.
* **Repositories (`@Repository`):** Responsible *only* for data persistence and retrieval. Do not include business rules in custom queries or repository implementations.
* **Mappers:** Use dedicated mapper classes or MapStruct to convert between Protobuf messages, Domain models, and JPA Entities. Do not bloat entities, stubs, or services with mapping logic.

### O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

*Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification.*

* **Strategy Pattern with Spring DI:** When multiple implementations or business rule variants exist (e.g., payment processing, notification channels, discount calculations), avoid large `if-else` or `switch` statements. Define a common interface and inject a `List<StrategyInterface>` or `Map<String, StrategyInterface>` via Spring's dependency injection to resolve implementations dynamically.
* **gRPC Interceptors (`ServerInterceptor`):** Handle cross-cutting transport concerns (authentication, logging, distributed tracing, and global exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` translation) via Spring-managed `ServerInterceptor` beans rather than repetitive `try-catch` blocks inside RPC methods.
* **Domain Events:** Use Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` and `@EventListener` (or `@TransactionalEventListener`) to decouple side effects (e.g., sending an email after user registration) from core business flows.

### L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

*Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.*

* **Contract Adherence:** Implementations of an interface must honor the expected behavior, preconditions, and postconditions of the interface.
* **No Unsupported Operations:** Never implement an interface method by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException`. If a class cannot fulfill the entire interface contract, the interface is too broad (see ISP).
* **Exception Consistency:** Subclasses or interface implementations should not throw unexpected checked or runtime exceptions that violate the caller's expectations of the base type.

### I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

*Clients should not be forced to depend upon interfaces that they do not use.*

* **Focused `.proto` Contracts:** Keep gRPC service definitions granular and domain-aligned (e.g., `UserQueryService`, `UserCommandService`) rather than monolithic `.proto` files with dozens of unrelated RPCs.
* **Role-Specific Java Interfaces:** Avoid bloated Java interfaces. Split them into focused interfaces based on client needs (e.g., `UserQueryUseCase`, `UserRegistrationUseCase`).
* **Repository Interfaces:** Do not blindly extend `JpaRepository` if a consumer only needs read access. Consider defining custom base repository interfaces (e.g., `ReadOnlyRepository<T, ID>`) exposing only `findById` and `findAll`.

### D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

*High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.*

* **Strict Boundary Isolation (Protobuf & JPA):** Never leak generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) or JPA `@Entity` classes into the core `application` or `domain` layers. Map both Protobuf messages and JPA Entities to/from pure Java domain models (`record` or domain classes) at the outer adapter boundaries.
* **Depend on Abstractions:** Core domain/business services must depend on interfaces (ports) rather than concrete infrastructure classes (adapters) like external gRPC stubs (`*BlockingStub`), REST clients, or third-party SDKs.

## 8. gRPC & Protocol Buffers Guidelines

* **Contract-First Development:** Place all `.proto` definitions in `src/main/proto/` organized by domain and version (e.g., `src/main/proto/user/v1/user.proto`).
* **Proto Options:** Always include `option java_multiple_files = true;` and a clear `option java_package = "...";` so generated classes are clean and modular. Never manually modify generated Java stub files under `target/generated-sources/` or `build/generated/`.
* **Protobuf Defaults & Presence:** Remember that `proto3` scalar fields default to zero-values (`0`, `""`, `false`) and cannot be `null`. Use the `optional` keyword or wrapper types in `.proto` when distinguishing between unset and default values is required by business logic.
* **Error Mapping:** Throw domain-specific exceptions in the service layer (e.g., `ResourceNotFoundException`, `InvalidArgumentDomainException`) and translate them centrally into appropriate `io.grpc.Status` codes (`Status.NOT_FOUND`, `Status.INVALID_ARGUMENT`, etc.) at the gRPC interceptor/advice boundary.

## 9. Recommended Package Structure

Organize packages by **feature/domain** using Hexagonal / Clean Architecture boundaries so transport (gRPC/REST) and persistence remain completely decoupled from business logic:

```text
src/main
├── proto
│   └── feature/v1              # .proto contract definitions
└── java/com/example/project
    ├── common                  # Shared utilities, interceptors, base configs
    │   ├── grpc                # Global gRPC ServerInterceptors & Status exception mappers
    │   └── config              # Security, gRPC, and Jackson configurations
    └── feature                 # e.g., order, user, payment
        ├── adapter             # Inbound & Outbound Adapters
        │   ├── in.grpc         # gRPC *ImplBase services & Protobuf Mappers
        │   ├── in.web          # (Optional) @RestController & HTTP DTOs
        │   └── out.persistence # JPA Entities, Spring Data Repositories, Entity Mappers
        ├── application         # @Service classes, Use Case implementations, Event Listeners
        └── domain              # Pure Java Domain Models, Records, Ports (Interfaces), Domain Exceptions
```

## 10. Coding Standards & Transactions

* **Transactions:** Place `@Transactional` on application service methods that modify state. Use `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for query-only service methods to optimize database performance.
* **Validation:** Validate incoming Protobuf requests immediately at the gRPC adapter boundary (or via `protovalidate` / custom validators) before invoking domain use cases. Enforce business invariants inside domain models.
* **Immutability:** Prefer `final` fields in all Spring beans and use Java `record` types for all internal commands, queries, domain value objects, and `@ConfigurationProperties`.

## 11. Testing Requirements

### Unit & Persistence Tests

* **Unit Tests:** Every new `@Service` and domain component must have fast, isolated unit tests using **JUnit 5** and **Mockito** (no Spring context or gRPC server loaded).
* **Persistence Tests:** Use `@DataJpaTest` and **Testcontainers** for repository integration tests …18 tokens truncated…rtThat(...)`) over standard JUnit assertions for better readability.

### gRPC Integration Testing (`@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport`)

* **In-Process Transport:** Annotate gRPC integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` to run the Spring gRPC server in-memory without binding to a network port.
* **Channel & Stub Wiring:** Inject `GrpcChannelFactory` into tests to create channels (`channels.createChannel("local")`) and wrap them with generated `*BlockingStub` clients.
* **Full Pipeline Coverage:** Do not call `*ImplBase` methods directly in integration tests. Always invoke RPCs through a gRPC stub so Protobuf serialization, `ServerInterceptor`s, and exception-to-`io.grpc.Status` mapping are verified end-to-end.
* **Error Assertions:** Assert gRPC error responses using `assertThrows(StatusRuntimeException.class, ...)` and verify both `ex.getStatus().getCode()` and `ex.getStatus().getDescription()`.

#### Reference Test Pattern

@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport
class UserGrpcIntegrationTest {

    @Autowired
    private GrpcChannelFactory channels;

    @Test
    void shouldReturnUser_whenValidIdProvided() {
        var stub = UserServiceGrpc.newBlockingStub(channels.createChannel("local"));

        UserResponse response = stub.getUser(
            GetUserRequest.newBuilder().setId("123").build()
        );

        assertThat(response.getName()).isEqualTo("Alice");
    }

## 12. Agent Execution Checklist

Before finalizing any code generation or modification, verify:

1. [ ] Are all dependencies injected via `private final` fields and a constructor?
2. [ ] Are generated Protobuf classes (`*Request`, `*Response`) and JPA `@Entity` classes completely isolated from the `domain` and `application` layers?
3. [ ] Are gRPC `*ImplBase` classes kept thin, delegating all business rules to application interfaces?
4. [ ] Are exceptions translated to `io.grpc.Status` centrally rather than via repetitive `try-catch` blocks in every RPC method?
5. [ ] Did you avoid speculative abstractions and only touch files directly required by the task?
6. [ ] Are unit tests and `@AutoConfigureInProcessTransport` gRPC stub integration tests included for all new endpoints and business logic?# AGENTS.md

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Merge with project-specific instructions as needed.

Tradeoff: These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.

1. Think Before Coding

Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs.

Before implementing:

State your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask.

If multiple interpretations exist, present them - don't pick silently.

If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted.

If something is unclear, stop. Name what's confusing. Ask.

2. Environment & Runtime

Ensure toolchain consistency before execution.

Always check for the presence of a .nvmrc file in the root directory.

Before installing dependencies, running scripts, or building the project, ensure the correct Node.js version is active in the current shell session:

export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"
[ -s "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" ] && \. "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"
nvm use


If nvm is not installed in the subshell, verify node -v matches .nvmrc before proceeding. If nvm use fails due to a missing local version, stop and log that nvm install is required.

3. Simplicity First

Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative.

No features beyond what was asked.

No abstractions for single-use code.

No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested.

No error handling for impossible scenarios.

If you write 200 lines and it could be 50, rewrite it.

Ask yourself: "Would a senior engineer say this is overcomplicated?" If yes, simplify.

4. Surgical Changes

Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.

When editing existing code:

Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.

Don't refactor things that aren't broken.

Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.

If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:

Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.

Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

5. Goal-Driven Execution

Define success criteria. Loop until verified.

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:

"Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"

"Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"

"Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
[Step] → verify: [check]

[Step] → verify: [check]

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.

6. TypeScript Style Guide

Strict typing and modern TypeScript conventions.

Strict Typing: Adhere to strict: true compiler rules. Explicitly type all variables, parameters, and return types where inference isn't structural or explicitly clear.

Functions & Methods: All exported functions, component props, and helper functions must include explicit parameter types and a return type annotation. Inline array callbacks (e.g., .map(), .filter()) may rely on contextual inference.

Modern Syntax: Prefer modern ESNext and TypeScript features. Use standard utility types like Record<string, unknown>, and union types like string | null or string | undefined.

Specificity: Avoid using any. If a type is genuinely dynamic or unknown, use unknown and narrow it downstream using type guards or conditional blocks. Use is predicates for custom type guards.

Interfaces vs. Types: Use interface for structural object definitions that benefit from declaration merging or extensions, and type for aliases, unions, intersections, or primitives.

7. Next.js & React Conventions

Routing: Follow the repository's existing routing structure (App Router vs. Pages Router—see docs/architecture.md). Do not mix router paradigms.

Server vs. Client Boundaries: When using App Router, default to React Server Components (RSC). Add 'use client' only when React hooks, browser APIs, or interactive event handlers are required, keeping client boundaries as close to leaf components as possible. Never import server-only modules or secrets into client components.

Data Fetching & State: Follow the project's established Apollo data-fetching and caching patterns rather than introducing ad-hoc fetch calls or new state management libraries.

Navigation & Media: Prefer next/link (<Link>) for internal navigation and next/image (<Image>) for images unless existing patterns dictate otherwise.

Environment Variables: Never expose server-only secrets or private API keys with the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix.

Check package.json for exact script names and use the repository's lockfile package manager (npm, pnpm, or yarn):

Typecheck: npm run typecheck (or npx tsc --noEmit)

Lint: npm run lint

Unit Tests (Jest): npm test -- <path-to-test>

E2E Tests (Cypress): npm run cypress:run

9. Testing

Unit test with Jest. Cover new features with e2e where feasible.

Write unit tests with Jest for new logic, components, and bug fixes.

Where a feature involves a user-facing flow, add or extend a Cypress e2e test (see cypress/) if feasible within the scope of the task.

# Frame Inventory Design System

A focused product design system extracted from the **Frame Inventory** prototype (an OOH out-of-home media operations tool). Built on top of the Global Design System (Global Next theme — Inter type, blue/cyan palette) and extended with the patterns this product introduced: inventory tables, master-data drawers, audit timelines, and stepper-driven creation flows.

## Sources
- `tokens.css` — full Global Design System tokens (Inter font, color palettes, semantic roles, spacing, elevation).
- `styles.css` — component styles built on top of the tokens (buttons, chips, tables, fields, surfaces, banners, timeline).
- `shell.jsx` — app chrome: rail nav, topbar, breadcrumbs, brand mark, icon set.
- `master-data.jsx`, `direction-a.jsx`, `direction-b.jsx` — production-shape examples consumed by the design system.

## Index
- `tokens.css` — design tokens (variables only — copy/import directly).
- `styles.css` — component styles built on those tokens.
- `preview/` — design-system preview cards (rendered in the Design System tab).
- `SKILL.md` — Agent Skill manifest for downstream prompting.
- `Frame Inventory.html` — the prototype that anchors the system.

## Content fundamentals
- **Tone**: operational, factual, second-person where action is required ("Add a frame", "Pick from master data"). Never marketing-y, never exclamatory.
- **Casing**: sentence case for everything — buttons (`New frame`, not `New Frame`), headers, table columns. Acronyms keep their caps (`OOH`, `CMS`, `DSP`).
- **Copy density**: short labels, longer help text below in `--text-secondary`. Inline microcopy preferred over modals.
- **No emoji** in product surfaces. Status uses iconographic dots/chips.
- **Numbers** are factual and contextual ("412 m", "10s · 6/min", "FRM-00214"). Use middle-dot `·` as a soft separator.

## Visual foundations
- **Type**: Inter, 13px body default — dense product UI, not document-style. Headings use the same family with weight (500–600) instead of size jumps.
- **Color**: cool blue primary (`--blue-1000` #046AC4) on near-white surfaces (`--gray-50`). Neutrals do the heavy lifting — color is reserved for status (green/red/orange) and primary actions.
- **Surfaces**: white cards on a `--gray-50` canvas, separated by 1px `--border-subtle` borders. **No drop shadows** on resting surfaces — elevation is reserved for popovers and drawers (`--elev-medium`).
- **Radii**: 4px (`--radius`) for inputs/buttons, 8px (`--radius-lg`) for surfaces, 999px for chips/pills.
- **Spacing**: 8px base — `--sp-1` through `--sp-10`. Most gaps are 16–24px (`--sp-2`, `--sp-3`).
- **Hover**: subtle background tint (`--gray-50` → `--blue-50`), no scale.
- **Press**: darker shade of the same token, no scale.
- **Borders**: 1px solid `--border-subtle` for surfaces, `--border-default` for inputs.
- **Animation**: practically none — drawers slide in 160ms, banners fade 120ms. Product is utilitarian; movement is reserved for state changes.
- **Imagery**: none in the chrome. The product is text- and data-first.
- **Iconography**: hand-rolled stroke icons at 1.8px stroke (Lucide-style), defined inline in `shell.jsx`. Domain glyphs (Station / Roadside / Airport / Mall / Bus Shelter) live alongside the UI icon set.

## Iconography
Inline SVG icons exported from `shell.jsx::Icon`. Stroke weight 1.8px, round caps/joins, single-color (`currentColor`). Domain icons are 16–24px. The system covers ~30 glyphs: `search`, `plus`, `pencil`, `trash`, `chev`, `chevL`, `filter`, `map`, `list`, `pin`, `history`, `more`, `link`, `warn`, `info`, `check`, `x`, `station`, `road`, `airport`, `mall`, `bus`, `frame`, `dash`, `cog`, `report`, `school`, `globe`, `download`, `upload`.

No emoji, no third-party icon CDN. If new icons are needed, draw new SVGs in the same stroke style.

## Caveats
- The system is **product-scoped** to Frame Inventory — not yet a brand-wide system.
- No marketing surfaces (landing pages, emails) are covered.
- Dark mode is not addressed.
- The "Inter via Google Fonts" fallback is in place but the WOFF2 files in `fonts/` are the source of truth.

# Bootstrap Orchestrator Persona

You are an expert repository documentation architect. Your task is to crawl
source code directories, partition trees into parallel processing scopes,
spawn worker subagents, format markdown files, perform correctness checks,
and compile Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) compliant README indexes per
[Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering](https://medium.com/@drensin/elephants-goldfish-and-the-new-golden-age-of-software-engineering-c33641a48874).

You must avoid writing functional source code and limit operations strictly
to documentation.

## Core Directives

1. **Strict Documentation Scope**: Limit operations exclusively to package contract
   (interface, invariant, and side-effect) and blueprint markdown files
   (defaulting to `README.md` or a configured `target_filename`) and
   documentation indexes. Do not create, modify, or refactor any functional source code.
2. **Recursive Partitioning**: Identify leaf components vs. intermediate architectural
   groupings. Partition large subtrees into independent worker partitions.
3. **Execution Modes**:
   - **Parallel Subagent Swarm**: Delegate subtree partitions to worker subagents for large trees (>5 directories).
   - **Direct Root Execution**: Process small subtrees (<= 5 directories) directly in the current thread.
4. **Contract Verification**: Verify that all generated contract files document public interfaces,
   invariants, system boundaries, and test commands accurately against the codebase.

# Core Mandates (Universal Goldfish Context)

You are a specialized Goldfish subagent operating within the Elephant-Goldfish Model. You have been delegated a specific task by the root agent (the Elephant).

1. **Strict Read-Only Protocol**: You are a strictly read-only agent. You have NO tools to modify the workspace, write files, or compile code. Do not attempt to fix or refactor any code.
2. **Stateless Mindset (Goldfish Isolation)**: You evaluate plans with zero conversational history or external assumptions. You must read the document as a naive team member or fresh reader who has just joined the project.
3. **No Chitchat**: Avoid conversational filler. Focus exclusively on technical rationale and findings. Do not narrate your tool usage.

---

# Role

You are **Codebase Details Goldfish**.
You are a pedantic, detail-oriented Technical Quality Auditor. You behave as a strict compliance officer who does not accept hand-waving explanations, unstated assumptions, or missing details. Your goal is to ensure the documentation perfectly and exhaustively matches the actual codebase implementation.

---

# Instructions

Inspect the `Mode` parameter specified by the caller:

### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM (Upstream Concept Ideation)
Evaluate the raw feature concept for observability, telemetry, and operational debuggability:
1. **Telemetry & Tracing**: Are key operations traceable in distributed tracing? Are telemetry metrics actionable?
2. **Operational Debuggability**: How will oncall engineers triage a production incident at 3 AM?
3. Report observability requirements and telemetry gaps back to the orchestrator.

### IF Mode: REVIEW (Document Audit)
Audit the target document file and line range specified by the caller:

1. **Map the Scope**: Parse the active target scope to identify which source files (from the provided codebase context) it describes.
2. **Verify Code vs. Doc**: For each mapped source file, read the code and verify that all key implementation details (including public APIs, core algorithms, configuration flags, and critical logic paths) are documented in the target scope.
3. **Audit against the Standard**: Compare the depth and accuracy of the descriptions in the target scope against the requirements defined in the Target Standard. Flag any areas that fall short of the standard's criteria.
4. **Filter Test Files**: Ignore simple unit test files, but strictly audit test infrastructure (mocks, helpers, base classes).

### Audit Vectors:
* **Missing Logic Detail**: Functions, validation rules, or algorithms present in the code that are omitted from the target scope.
* **Unstated Assumptions**: Hardcoded constants, environment variables, or system dependencies in the code that are not documented.
* **Undocumented Edge Cases**: Catch blocks, null checks, retry limits, or failure modes in the code that are missing in the target scope.
* **Test Infrastructure Neglect**: Ensuring that shared mocks and test helpers are documented with the same level of detail as production code.
* **Contradicts the Code**: The document describes current behavior that the source does not have. Report as 🔴 Blocker: every later reader inherits the false statement.
* **Non-Existent References**: Files, functions, endpoints, or tables that the document cites as current state but that do not exist. Check every one.

**Proposed files are not findings.** An implementation plan lists files it will create. Their absence is not a defect. Apply Non-Existent References only to items the document says exist now. If the plan lists files without marking each `Create`, `Modify`, or `Delete`, report that once as 🟡 Major, and do not flag each path.

---

# Output Format

Report your findings back to the orchestrator in plain, natural language.

#### IF Mode: REVIEW
For each finding, include:
1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
2. **Affected Scope**: Referenced filepath, API, or line numbers.
3. **Discrepancy Description & Rationale**: Explanation of the codebase drift or existing library reuse opportunity discovered via code search.

#### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM
For each telemetry or debuggability gap, include:
1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
2. **Dimension**: Observability & Operational SRE Debuggability
3. **Operational Risk**: Missing trace context, unmonitored metric, or triage friction.
4. **Mitigation Requirement**: Mandatory telemetry requirement for the Concepts Brief/PRD.

# Frontend (Next.js)

## Overview

Next.js (App Router), React 19, and TypeScript serve the exercise’s backend
health check page.

## Interface

- The Next.js rewrite matches `/api/:path*` and preserves the API path at the backend. [next.config.ts:rewrites]
- The package exposes `dev`, `build`, `start`, and `lint` scripts. [package.json:scripts]
- [Application source](./src/README.md) contains the App Router layout and health check page.

## Invariants

- `BACKEND_URL` sets the backend origin and defaults to `http://localhost:8080`. [next.config.ts:backendUrl]

## Side Effects

- Next.js forwards matching `/api/:path*` requests to the configured backend. [next.config.ts:rewrites]

## Local Development

Run these commands from `src/frontend`.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

## Verification

- Run `npm run lint` from `src/frontend`. [package.json:scripts.lint]
# Frontend Source

## Overview

This directory groups the frontend application source under the Next.js App
Router.

## Subdirectories & Boundaries

- [App Router](./app/README.md) owns the root layout and the frontend page that checks backend health.
# App Router

## Overview

The root layout wraps the app. The home page displays the outcome of a backend
health check.

## Interface

- `RootLayout` renders route content within an English-language HTML document. `metadata` sets the page title and favicon. [layout.tsx:RootLayout] [layout.tsx:metadata]
- `Home` renders `/` and shows a loading message, the returned JSON, or an error message. [page.tsx:Home] [page.tsx:FetchState]

## Invariants

- The frontend types the health response with string fields for `status`, `service`, and `timestamp`. [page.tsx:HealthResponse]
- An HTTP response outside the 2xx range enters the error state. [page.tsx:Home]

## Side Effects

- `Home` requests `/api/health` on mount and updates the displayed state when the request resolves or fails. [page.tsx:Home]
- Cleanup aborts the request, and the error handler ignores `AbortError`. [page.tsx:Home]

## Verification

- Run `npm run lint` from `src/frontend`. [../../package.json:scripts.lint]
- With both services running, open `/` and confirm the page displays the backend health response. [page.tsx:Home]

# Frame inventory application

## Overview

This package contains the Spring Boot entry point and the HTTP health endpoint.

## Interface

- `Application.main(String[] args)` starts the Spring Boot application. [Application.java:main]
- `GET /api/health` returns the backend's status, service name, and timestamp. [HealthController.java:health]

## Invariants

- The health response has `status` set to `UP`, `service` set to `frame-inventory-backend`, and `timestamp` set to the string form of the current `Instant`. [HealthController.java:health]
- The controller allows cross-origin requests from any origin. [HealthController.java:@CrossOrigin]

## Side Effects

- `Application.main` delegates startup to `SpringApplication.run`. [Application.java:main]
- The health handler reads the system clock to build its response. [HealthController.java:health]

## Verification

From `src/backend`, run `./gradlew test`.

# Frame Inventory Design System

## Overview

The design system supports the Frame Inventory prototype for out-of-home media operations. It builds on the Global Design System’s Global Next theme with Inter typography and a blue and cyan palette. It adds inventory tables, master data drawers, audit timelines and a step-by-step creation flow.

The [design skill](./SKILL.md) describes how to reuse these patterns. The HTML cards in `preview/` show individual design tokens and components.

## Interface

- Open [Frame Inventory.html](./Frame%20Inventory.html) for the prototype. It loads React, ReactDOM and Babel from a CDN, then local JSX scripts and CSS. `App` mounts into `#root`. `[Frame Inventory.html:script]` `[app.jsx:App]`
- Load `tokens.css` before `styles.css`. The first defines fonts, color, typography, spacing and elevation. The second styles the shell, buttons, fields, inventory tables, chips and timelines. `[tokens.css::root]` `[styles.css:.app]` `[styles.css:.btn]` `[styles.css:.field]` `[styles.css:.tbl]` `[styles.css:.chip]` `[styles.css:.timeline]`
- `window.FRAME_DATA` exposes sample frames, status metadata, fixture-derived filter options and map pin positions. The shell exposes shared browser components including `Icon`, `Rail`, `Topbar`, `FrameMap`, `Timeline` and `ExternalIdsTable`. `[data.jsx:window.FRAME_DATA]` `[shell.jsx:Object.assign]`
- Direction A offers a filter sidebar and table or map, with separate detail and edit screens and a history tab. Its text search includes external ID values. Direction B keeps a searchable, site-filtered list beside a pane that switches between map, detail, edit and history. `[direction-a.jsx:DirA]` `[direction-a.jsx:DirA_Search]` `[direction-a.jsx:DirA_Detail]` `[direction-b.jsx:DirB]`
- The new frame wizard has five steps from Basics through Review. The master data rail opens regions and towns, site types, formats and external ID systems via `md-regions`, `md-sites`, `md-formats` and `md-extids`. `[master-data.jsx:NewFrameScreen]` `[master-data.jsx:MD_CONTENT]` `[shell.jsx:Rail]`

## Invariants

- The app starts in Direction A with comfortable density and the search screen. Switching direction returns to the frame search screen. Shortcuts 1–4 select screens and A/B selects direction when focus is outside inputs, textareas and selects. `[app.jsx:DEFAULT_TWEAKS]` `[app.jsx:App]`
- Both directions initialize selection to `FRM-00214` and fall back to the first fixture if the selection cannot be resolved. Direction A uses the same filtered results for its table and map. Direction B retains its list controls while switching panes. `[direction-a.jsx:DirA]` `[direction-a.jsx:DirA_Search]` `[direction-b.jsx:DirB]`
- The wizard starts with `draft` status and the first region, site type and technology from `window.FRAME_DATA`. `[master-data.jsx:NewFrameScreen]`

## Side Effects

- Script initialization fills empty fixture histories with sample events and publishes the shared data and components as browser globals. `[data.jsx:FRAMES.forEach]` `[data.jsx:window.FRAME_DATA]` `[shell.jsx:Object.assign]` `[direction-a.jsx:window.DirA]` `[direction-b.jsx:window.DirB]` `[master-data.jsx:Object.assign]`
- Frame edit Save changes and Cancel both return to detail. Save as draft and the external ID link, edit and unlink controls have no handlers. These controls leave the fixture records and history unchanged. `[direction-a.jsx:DirA_Edit]` `[direction-b.jsx:DirB_Edit]` `[direction-b.jsx:DirB]` `[shell.jsx:ExternalIdsTable]`
- Create frame passes the in-memory draft to `onCreate(draft)`. The app returns to the frame section without adding a record. Master data Create and Save changes only close the drawer. Delete has no handler. `[master-data.jsx:NewFrameScreen]` `[master-data.jsx:MDDrawer]` `[master-data.jsx:MasterDataScreen]` `[app.jsx:App]`
- Tweak changes update React state, send `__edit_mode_set_keys` to the parent window and dispatch `tweakchange` in the current window. The panel listens for host activation and deactivation, reads `deck-stage.railVisible` from local storage, and sends `__deck_rail_visible` to the current window when toggled. These hooks make no local storage writes. `[tweaks-panel.jsx:useTweaks]` `[tweaks-panel.jsx:TweaksPanel]`

## Verification

Run this command from the repository root.

```sh
python3 -m http.server 8000 --directory design-system
```

Open [the local prototype](http://localhost:8000/Frame%20Inventory.html) in a browser that can reach the CDN scripts. Use the A/B controls to switch directions, filter the frames, and open a frame from the list and map. Open the edit screen and confirm that Save changes returns to detail with the fixture values. Complete the New frame wizard and open a master data drawer to check that Create returns to the existing fixture view.

## Content fundamentals

- Use a factual, operational tone and second person where an action is required. Examples include “Add a frame” and “Pick from master data”.
- Use sentence case for buttons, headings and columns. Keep acronyms such as OOH, CMS and DSP uppercase.
- Keep labels short and put longer help below them in `--text-secondary`. Prefer inline help.
- Keep product surfaces free of emoji. Use dots and chips for status.
- Give numbers context, such as `412 m`, `10s · 6/min` and `FRM-00214`. Use a middle dot to separate related details.

## Visual foundations

- Use Inter at 13px for dense body copy. Use weights 500–600 to distinguish headings.
- Use `--blue-1000` (#046AC4) for primary actions. Use near-white and cool neutrals for the canvas, with green, red and orange for status.
- Place white cards on the near-white canvas. Use 1px `--border-subtle` borders on resting surfaces and `--border-default` on inputs. Reserve elevation for popovers and drawers.
- Use `--radius` (4px) for inputs and buttons, `--radius-lg` (8px) for surfaces, and `--radius-pill` (999px) for chips and pills.
- Use an 8px spacing base. Use `--sp-2` or `--sp-3` for typical gaps of 16px or 24px.
- Use a subtle tint on hover and a darker tint when pressed. Keep control dimensions steady and reserve motion for state changes.
- Keep app chrome focused on text and data. Use the existing inline SVG icons from `shell.jsx` as the reference for new glyphs. Use a 1.8px stroke, round caps and joins, and `currentColor`. Size domain glyphs at 16–24px.

## Caveats

The system covers Frame Inventory operational screens. Marketing surfaces and dark mode are outside its scope.

`tokens.css` loads local TrueType Inter files at weights 400, 500, 600 and 700. Keep the relative `fonts/` paths when reusing the stylesheet. The font stack falls back to the platform sans serif and Arial. `[tokens.css:@font-face]` `[tokens.css:--font-sans]`

+## Overview

+The design system supports the Frame Inventory prototype for out-of-home media operations. It builds on the Global Design System’s Global Next theme with Inter typography and a blue and cyan palette. It adds inventory tables, master data drawers, audit timelines and a step-by-step creation flow.

 ## Content fundamentals
-- **Tone**: operational, factual, second-person where action is required ("Add a frame", "Pick from master data"). Never marketing-y, never exclamatory.
-- **Casing**: sentence case for everything — buttons (`New frame`, not `New Frame`), headers, table columns. Acronyms keep their caps (`OOH`, `CMS`, `DSP`).

 ## Visual foundations
-- **Type**: Inter, 13px body default — dense product UI, not document-style. Headings use the same family with weight (500–600) instead of size jumps.
-- **Color**: cool blue primary (`--blue-1000` #046AC4) on near-white surfaces (`--gray-50`). Neutrals do the heavy lifting — color is reserved for status (green/red/orange) and primary actions.
-- **Surfaces**: white cards on a `--gray-50` canvas, separated by 1px `--border-subtle` borders. **No drop shadows** on resting surfaces — elevation is reserved for popovers and drawers (`--elev-medium`).
-- **Radii**: 4px (`--radius`) for inputs/buttons, 8px (`--radius-lg`) for surfaces, 999px for chips/pills.
-- **Spacing**: 8px base — `--sp-1` through `--sp-10`. Most gaps are 16–24px (`--sp-2`, `--sp-3`).
-- **Hover**: subtle background tint (`--gray-50` → `--blue-50`), no scale.

-- **Borders**: 1px solid `--border-subtle` for surfaces, `--border-default` for inputs.
-- **Animation**: practically none — drawers slide in 160ms, banners fade 120ms. Product is utilitarian; movement is reserved for state changes.
-- **Imagery**: none in the chrome. The product is text- and data-first.
-- **Iconography**: hand-rolled stroke icons at 1.8px stroke (Lucide-style), defined inline in `shell.jsx`. Domain glyphs (Station / Roadside / Airport / Mall / Bus Shelter) live alongside the UI icon set.
+
+- Use the Inter type scale. Body copy defaults to `--fs-body2` (14px), with 13px for dense UI elements. Use weights 500–600 to distinguish headings.
+- Use `--blue-1000` (#046AC4) for primary actions. Use near-white and cool neutrals for the canvas, with green, red and orange for status.
+- Place white cards on the near-white canvas. Use 1px `--border-subtle` borders on resting surfaces and `--border-default` on inputs. Reserve elevation for popovers and drawers.
+- Use `--radius` (4px) for inputs and buttons, `--radius-lg` (8px) for surfaces, and `--radius-pill` (999px) for chips and pills.
+- Use an 8px spacing base. Use `--sp-2` or `--sp-3` for typical gaps of 16px or 24px.
+- Use a subtle tint on hover and a darker tint when pressed. Keep control dimensions steady and reserve motion for state changes.
+- Keep app chrome focused on text and data.
 
 ## Iconography
-Inline SVG icons exported from `shell.jsx::Icon`. Stroke weight 1.8px, round caps/joins, single-color (`currentColor`). Domain icons are 16–24px. +
+- Actions and navigation include `search`, `plus`, `pencil`, `trash`, `chev`, `chevL`, `filter`, `download`, `upload`, `map`, `list`, `pin`, `history`, `more`, `link`, `warn`, `info`, `check` and `x`.
+- Domain glyphs include `station`, `road`, `airport`, `mall`, `bus`, `frame`, `dash`, `cog`, `report`, `school` and `globe`.
 
 ## Caveats
-- The system is **product-scoped** to Frame Inventory — not yet a brand-wide system.
-- No marketing surfaces (landing pages, emails) are covered.
-- Dark mode is not addressed.
-- The "Inter via Google Fonts" fallback is in place but the WOFF2 files in `fonts/` are the source of truth.
+
+The system covers Frame Inventory operational screens. Marketing surfaces and dark mode are outside its scope.

+- Use a factual, operational tone and second person where an action is required. Examples include “Add a frame” and “Pick from master data”.
+- Use sentence case for buttons, headings and columns. Keep acronyms such as OOH, CMS and DSP uppercase.
+- Keep labels short and put longer help below them in `--text-secondary`. Prefer inline help.
+- Keep product surfaces free of emoji. Use dots and chips for status.
+- Give numbers context, such as `412 m`, `10s · 6/min` and `FRM-00214`. Use a middle dot to separate related details.
 
 ## Visual foundations
-- **Type**: Inter, 13px body default — dense product UI, not document-style. Headings use the same family with weight (500–600) instead of size jumps.
-- **Color**: cool blue primary (`--blue-1000` #046AC4) on near-white surfaces (`--gray-50`). Neutrals do the heavy lifting — color is reserved for status (green/red/orange) and primary actions.
-- **Surfaces**: white cards on a `--gray-50` canvas, separated by 1px `--border-subtle` borders. **No drop shadows** on resting surfaces — elevation is reserved for popovers and drawers (`--elev-medium`).
-- **Radii**: 4px (`--radius`) for inputs/buttons, 8px (`--radius-lg`) for surfaces, 999px for chips/pills.
-- **Spacing**: 8px base — `--sp-1` through `--sp-10`. Most gaps are 16–24px (`--sp-2`, `--sp-3`).
-- **Hover**: subtle background tint (`--gray-50` → `--blue-50`), no scale.
-- **Press**: darker shade of the same token, no scale.
-- **Borders**: 1px solid `--border-subtle` for surfaces, `--border-default` for inputs.
-- **Animation**: practically none — drawers slide in 160ms, banners fade 120ms. Product is utilitarian; movement is reserved for state changes.
-- **Imagery**: none in the chrome. The product is text- and data-first.
-- **Iconography**: hand-rolled stroke icons at 1.8px stroke (Lucide-style), defined inline in `shell.jsx`. Domain glyphs (Station / Roadside / Airport / Mall / Bus Shelter) live alongside the UI icon set.
+
+- Use the Inter type scale. Body copy defaults to `--fs-body2` (14px), with 13px for dense UI elements. Use weights 500–600 to distinguish headings.
+- Use `--blue-1000` (#046AC4) for primary actions. Use near-white and cool neutrals for the canvas, with green, red and orange for status.
+- Place white cards on the near-white canvas. Use 1px `--border-subtle` borders on resting surfaces and `--border-default` on inputs. Reserve elevation for popovers and drawers.
+- Use `--radius` (4px) for inputs and buttons, `--radius-lg` (8px) for surfaces, and `--radius-pill` (999px) for chips and pills.
+- Use an 8px spacing base. Use `--sp-2` or `--sp-3` for typical gaps of 16px or 24px.
+- Use a subtle tint on hover and a darker tint when pressed. Keep control dimensions steady and reserve motion for state changes.
+- Keep app chrome focused on text and data.
 
 ## Iconography
-Inline SVG icons exported from `shell.jsx::Icon`. Stroke weight 1.8px, round caps/joins, single-color (`currentColor`). Domain icons are 16–24px. The system covers ~30 glyphs: `search`, `plus`, `pencil`, `trash`, `chev`, `chevL`, `filter`, `map`, `list`, `pin`, `history`, `more`, `link`, `warn`, `info`, `check`, `x`, `station`, `road`, `airport`, `mall`, `bus`, `frame`, `dash`, `cog`, `report`, `school`, `globe`, `download`, `upload`.
 
-No emoji, no third-party icon CDN. If new icons are needed, draw new SVGs in the same stroke style.
+Use the inline SVGs in `shell.jsx` as the reference for new glyphs. Use a 1.8px stroke, round caps and joins, and `currentColor`. Size domain glyphs at 16–24px. `[shell.jsx:Icon]` `[shell.jsx:SiteIcon]`
+
+- Actions and navigation include `search`, `plus`, `pencil`, `trash`, `chev`, `chevL`, `filter`, `download`, `upload`, `map`, `list`, `pin`, `history`, `more`, `link`, `warn`, `info`, `check` and `x`.
+- Domain glyphs include `station`, `road`, `airport`, `mall`, `bus`, `frame`, `dash`, `cog`, `report`, `school` and `globe`.
 
 ## Caveats
-- The system is **product-scoped** to Frame Inventory — not yet a brand-wide system.
-- No marketing surfaces (landing pages, emails) are covered.
-- Dark mode is not addressed.
-- The "Inter via Google Fonts" fallback is in place but the WOFF2 files in `fonts/` are the source of truth.
+
+The system covers Frame Inventory operational screens. Marketing surfaces and dark mode are outside its scope.
+
+`tokens.css` loads local TrueType Inter files at weights 400, 500, 600 and 700. Keep the relative `fonts/` paths when reusing the stylesheet. The font stack falls back to the platform sans serif and Arial. `[tokens.css:@font-face]` `[tokens.css:--font-sans]`

license: Apache-2.0
disable-model-invocation: true
description: >-
  Runs drift detection on all design documents to check for document and
  code consistency. Produces an actionable report with differences. Use when the
  user asks to detect drift or check for consistency across all design documents
  or READMEs in a directory.
---

# Detect Drift In Designs and Code

When running in Codex or ChatGPT Work, first read [Codex integration](../../docs/codex.md).
In Claude Code or Cowork, read `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/docs/claude.md` first.

When the user asks to detect drift across all designs or a set of READMEs, the
goal is to identify all instances where the codebase has diverged or failed to
implement the specifications described by those designs or READMEs.

1.  **Check Input**: Verify a directory containing design documents or READMEs
    is provided. If not provided, ask the user to specify the target directory.
2.  **List Documents**: List all files in the design directory.
3.  **Analyze**: For EACH design document:

    *   **Contextualize**: Read the design document. Identify the intent,
        proposed changes, and specific filenames/symbols mentioned.
    *   **Locate Source**: Find the corresponding source code files in the
        source tree. If paths aren't explicit, use code search or grep to
        locate the relevant classes, functions, or API endpoints mentioned in
        the doc. Prompt the user to add missing links to the document to make
        future detection cheaper.
    *   **Verify**: Read the current state of those source files.
    *   **Detect Drift**: Compare the design vs. reality. Look specifically for:
        *   Missing Features: Logic described in the doc but absent in the code.
        *   Incomplete Models: Dataclasses/Classes/Structs/Protos missing fields
            specified in the design.
        *   Logic Shortcuts: Hardcoded values where dynamic logic was planned.
        *   Architectural Divergence: Implementation using different
            patterns/libraries than proposed.
    *   **Filter**: Report ONLY the differences. Do not describe what is working
        or what matches. If the code matches the design perfectly, output "No
        drift detected."

4.  **Report**: Produce a single report listing all discrepancies found.

    *   Append the analysis for each file to `{YYYY-MM-DD}_DRIFT_REPORT.md`
        using your file-writing tool.
    *   Strict Format:

        ```markdown
        ## <DESIGN_DOC_NAME>

        <Bulleted list of specific divergences found>
        <Or "No drift detected">
        ```

5.  **Guidance**

    -   Be rigorous. If a design doc mentions a specific object, field or file
        name and the code doesn't have it, that is a reportable drift. Double
        check for coverage. If there is some part of the logic that is not
        referenced in a design or README, this is a reportable drift.
    -   Read files liberally to ensure you are looking at the current state
        of the code, not relying on memory.
    -   Process the files sequentially to ensure the tool output buffer doesn't
        overflow.

# Codex integration

## Install and locate the plugin

For the desktop app, install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357). This listing is desktop-only.

For Codex CLI, install the whole plugin, including its personas and standards:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add google/elephant-goldfish-model
codex plugin add egm@egm
```

Start a fresh session after installation. Select the installed `egm` skill
from the available skills. Use its discovered absolute `SKILL.md` path;
do not assume a particular cache directory, version, or checkout location.

From `<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`, the plugin root is three parent
directories above the file. Resolve bundled `agents/`, `resources/`, and
`docs/` paths against that root. Resolve `references/` against the active
skill's directory. Resolve user documents and generated artifacts against
the user's working directory. Never substitute similarly named files in the
user's project for bundled personas or standards.

If the user's prompt or agent instructions file (`AGENTS.md`) has a line
`EGM artifact directory: <path>`, write briefs, drafts, and reports to that
folder. Resolve a relative path against the working directory. If a path from
`AGENTS.md` resolves outside the working directory, after following symbolic
links, ask the user to confirm it before creating the folder or writing there.
If they decline or no one can confirm, use the working directory and say why.
Create the folder if it does not exist.

In ChatGPT Work, a skill may be exposed through a cloud resource identifier
while supporting files live in the installed local bundle. Use the installed
path supplied by the skill inventory or installation metadata for those files;
do not construct cloud resource identifiers for arbitrary supporting paths.
If no installed path is available, report the missing capability instead of
guessing a cache location. Read reviewer filenames and frontmatter from the
bundle: a role such as `egm-design` maps to `agents/design_critic.md`, not
`agents/design.md`. Confirm each resolved path before dispatch.

## Fresh-context reviewers

Inspect the available native subagent tool schema. Tool names can be
namespaced and vary by Codex version. When `spawn_agent` exposes
`fork_context`, explicitly set `fork_context: false` for every Goldfish.
When the schema instead exposes `fork_turns`, use `fork_turns: "none"`.
This applies to reviewers launched by a synthesizer too. Use a general-purpose agent
and pass absolute paths to the persona, standards, target document, and
explicitly selected reading list. Do not pass the parent transcript, private
reasoning, or answers the document is supposed to explain.

Require the reviewer to read its persona, target, and every supplied standard
before returning findings. A missing read or inaccessible file is an incomplete
review, not a clean result. Verify native tool results when the host exposes
them; a parent-written completion summary is not equivalent evidence.

Wait for actual reviewer completion before synthesizing findings. Propagate
failures and timeouts; a launched reviewer is not a completed review. If
nesting is unavailable, dispatch reviewers directly from the parent while
preserving the same isolation. If the available tool cannot establish a fresh
context, stop the Goldfish review and report that limitation.

Fresh conversation context does not isolate the filesystem, configured memory
services, or project instructions. Do not retrieve conversation history or
memory to supply missing design context. An isolation test should use a unique
parent-only marker and check the actual child result, not the parent's claim.

The `fork_context: false` and `fork_turns: "none"` options concern parent
conversation turns. They do not prove that Codex excludes host instruction
files. Issue [#237](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/issues/237)
reports that Codex CLI 0.166.0 injected project and user `AGENTS.md` files
despite `fork_turns: "none"`. Treat instruction-file exclusion as unverified
unless a separate child-context probe confirms it for the tested host version.

## Questions and artifacts

The shared skills' question payloads describe the intended interaction, not a
literal Codex API. Use a structured question tool only when it is available
and permitted in the current mode, mapping to its actual schema. Otherwise
ask one plain-text question and wait for the answer. Preserve the skill's
readiness and section approval gates; tool unavailability is not approval.

Link generated artifacts with absolute-path Markdown links such as
`[design draft](/absolute/project/design_draft.md)`. For paths containing
spaces use `[design draft](</absolute/my project/design_draft.md>)`.
Do not use `file://` links in Codex chat.

## Verification

Run the offline packaging checks with `pytest tests/unit`. The opt-in native
workflow tests are documented in [TESTING.md](https://github.com/google/elephant-goldfish-model/blob/main/TESTING.md). They require
an authenticated Codex CLI and consume model usage. Installing or discovering
the plugin alone does not establish end-to-end workflow support.

## ChatGPT

Install the [published EGM plugin](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6aeb90f47ec88191a3c107e01d3eb357) in the ChatGPT desktop app. This listing is desktop-only; it does not establish support for cloud Work sessions.

### Test a local package

For personal testing, open Plugins > Add > Upload plugin archive in ChatGPT.
Package the runtime files from the repository root:

```sh
python3 scripts/pack_plugin.py --target openai --output /tmp/egm-chatgpt
```

Use a fresh output directory. Upload `/tmp/egm-chatgpt/egm-openai.zip` and

*** Add File: 2026-11-26_DRIFT_REPORT.md
+# EGM drift report
+
+## README.md
+
+- The system boundaries omit the Compose startup order and development mounts. Compose starts PostgreSQL and OpenSearch before the backend, starts the backend before the frontend, and bind-mounts the frontend's \`src\` and \`public\` directories. Document startup order separately from runtime calls. [Compose service definitions](./docker-compose.yml#L15-L44)
+- The service table describes PostgreSQL as provisioned for frame data. Add that the current backend has neither a PostgreSQL nor an OpenSearch client and that its custom health response uses a fixed status and the system clock. This clarifies what a successful smoke check verifies. [Backend dependencies](./src/backend/build.gradle#L20-L26) [Health handler](./src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/HealthController.java#L16-L23)
+- The non-Docker backend instructions show the command but omit the JDK prerequisite. State that the Gradle build targets Java 21. [Local run instructions](./README.md#L61-L68) [Gradle toolchain](./src/backend/build.gradle#L10-L14)
+
+## design-system/README.md
+
+- The Interface section omits the standalone HTML entry point. Add a link and describe how it unpacks bundled assets in the browser. The source HTML entry point described in the README loads its runtime scripts from a CDN. [Standalone loader](./design-system/Frame%20Inventory%20%28standalone%29.html#L59-L112) [Source HTML entry point](./design-system/Frame%20Inventory.html#L7-L11)
+- Direction A's filter contract omits the default status selection and the inclusive 0–5,000 m school-distance range. Direction B uses its filtered list for map pins as well. Document these behaviors where the README describes how the two views filter fixtures. [Direction A filter logic](./design-system/direction-a.jsx#L47-L78) [Direction B map](./design-system/direction-b.jsx#L120-L125)
+- Both history screens always pass the full fixture history to \`Timeline\`. The history filter selectors have no change handler. Describe the selectors as prototype controls so readers can distinguish the history display from functional filtering. [Direction A history](./design-system/direction-a.jsx#L325-L343) [Direction B history](./design-system/direction-b.jsx#L313-L332)
+- The new-frame section omits that users can jump directly to Review and invoke Create without a field-validation gate. The wizard also says a frame receives an ID on save, although the app callback only navigates back to Frames. Document those limits where the README describes the create flow. [Wizard navigation](./design-system/master-data.jsx#L22-L56) [Create handler](./design-system/master-data.jsx#L185-L201) [App callback](./design-system/app.jsx#L56-L63)
+- The host messaging contract omits the panel's \`__edit_mode_available\` and \`__edit_mode_dismissed\` messages. Record them alongside activation, deactivation, and tweak updates. [Panel messaging](./design-system/tweaks-panel.jsx#L251-L265)
+- The iconography guidance gives 1.8px as the stroke width. Existing icons such as \`plus\`, \`chev\`, \`check\`, and \`x\` use 2px. Label 1.8px as the default for new icons. [Icon definitions](./design-system/shell.jsx#L6-L25)
+
+## src/README.md
+
+No drift detected.
+
+## src/backend/README.md
+
+- The verification section gives the Gradle test command without describing its coverage. The current suite checks application context startup. The HTTP endpoint has a separate manual smoke check. Link that check from this section. [Backend test](./src/backend/src/test/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/ApplicationTests.java#L6-L12) [Repository smoke check](./README.md#L54-L59)
+
+## src/backend/src/README.md
+
+- The overview refers to Gradle source sets, but the boundary list covers only production sources. Mention the test source set and link to the context-load test, which has no directory contract of its own. [Backend test](./src/backend/src/test/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/ApplicationTests.java#L6-L12)
+
+## src/backend/src/main/README.md
+
+- The runtime configuration summary omits \`spring.application.name\`. Add its value, \`frame-inventory-backend\`, alongside the server port and Actuator exposure settings. [Spring configuration](./src/backend/src/main/resources/application.yml#L1-L12)

+## src/frontend/README.md
+
+- The frontend contract covers local scripts and API rewrites but omits its container entry point. Document the Node 22 Alpine image and the dev server binding to \`0.0.0.0:3000\`. [Frontend Dockerfile](./src/frontend/Dockerfile#L1-L7)
