+# Frame inventory schema and version history
+
+**Author** Alex Callow  
+**Date** 2026-11-26
+
+## Overview
+
+Use PostgreSQL to store frames and their accepted versions. Each \`frame_id\` identifies one frame through successive uploads. An incoming row whose \`modified_date\` is strictly older than the current row is ignored. An equal or newer value closes the previous version and opens the next version at the same import instant.
+
+The supplied extract has 1,000 rows, 1,000 distinct frame IDs, and 45 fields. The migration will create the schema on Spring Boot startup. The exercise calls for a user-driven CSV upload, so the migration will start with empty inventory tables. [CSV](./data/inventory_frame.csv) [Exercise requirements](./INSTRUCTIONS.md#L52-L64)
+
+## Analysis
+
+### Raw field mapping
+
+CSV values arrive as text. The types below describe how to parse them for PostgreSQL. A blank optional value becomes SQL \`NULL\`. Observed null counts and value sets describe this extract.
+
+| CSV fields | Observed representation | Proposed PostgreSQL mapping |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| \`frame_id\` | Ten decimal digits, unique and populated in all rows | \`frame.frame_id text\` primary key. The prototype also uses alphanumeric frame IDs. |
+| \`created_date\`, \`modified_date\` | Date and time to seconds, without offsets | \`frame_version\` source timestamps, \`timestamp without time zone\`. |
+| \`country_code\`, \`region\`, \`town\` | Codes and names. One country, 12 regions, 172 towns | Country code and region name form the region's natural key. Town name is scoped to a region. Each table also has a generated primary key. |
+| \`postcode\` | UK postcode with a space, 484 distinct | \`postcode\` row keyed by generated ID, unique on \`(town_id, postcode)\`. |
+| \`postcode_area\`, \`postcode_district\`, \`postcode_sector\`, \`postcode_unit\` | Text fragments, some containing letters | Derive from the postcode. The four fragments reconstruct it exactly in all 1,000 rows. |
+| \`longitude\`, \`latitude\` | Signed decimal degrees | Exact \`numeric\` columns on \`frame_version\`, with valid coordinate ranges. |
+| \`location\` | \`POINT (latitude longitude)\` text | Derive from the scalar coordinates if an export requires the legacy format. All 1,000 rows contain the same pair in this order. |
+| \`site_no\`, \`inventory_site_no\`, \`panel_number\` | Identifiers. Site and panel numbers can contain leading zeros | Independent \`text\` fields on \`frame_version\`. |
+| \`location_id\` | Identifier, 13 blanks | Nullable \`text\` on \`frame_version\`. In 67 rows the populated value differs from the normalized postcode. |
+| \`environment\`, \`address\`, \`station\`, \`airport\` | Text. Station has 593 blanks and airport has 887 | \`text\` on \`frame_version\`, with the optional site names nullable. |
+| \`type_classic_digital\`, \`format\`, \`size_group_code\` | Codes. Nine distinct combinations | \`frame_format\` row keyed by generated ID, unique on the three codes. Codes stay as text, including size groups such as \`006\`. |
+| \`size_code\`, \`aspect_ratio_code\`, \`t_size\` | Codes and labels. \`t_size\` has 57 blanks | \`text\` columns on \`frame_version\`. |
+| \`pixel_height\`, \`pixel_width\` | Positive integers, 28 blanks in each column | Nullable \`integer\` dimensions on \`frame_version\`. |
+| \`illumination_type_id\`, \`number_of_slots\`, \`distance_to_closest_school\` | Integer code and counts or distances | \`integer\` on \`frame_version\`. The proposed distance unit is metres, consistent with the prototype. |
+| \`status\`, \`status_reason\` | Text. Every row is \`LIVE\` and all reasons are blank | Status and nullable reason on \`frame_version\`. |
+| \`impact_weight\` | Decimal, six blanks | Nullable exact \`numeric\` on \`frame_version\`. |
+| \`premium\` | \`0\` or \`1\` | \`boolean\` on \`frame_version\`. |
+| \`production_rate_card\`, \`production_rate_card_legacy\` | Both columns are blank throughout | Separate nullable \`text\` fields until the source contract establishes how they relate. |
+| \`pricing_grade\` | Text, 869 blanks | Nullable \`text\` on \`frame_version\`. |
+| \`price_entity_id\`, \`broadsign_display_unit_id\`, \`broadsign_frame_id\`, \`broadsign_domain_id\` | Opaque codes. Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | \`frame_version_external_reference\` rows keyed by \`(version_id, reference_type)\`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
+| \`linked_frame_ids\` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered \`frame_version_link\` rows keyed by \`(version_id, position)\`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |
+
+### Relational boundaries
+
+- \`frame_version\` has its own primary key and foreign keys to \`frame\`, \`postcode\`, and \`frame_format\`. \`postcode\` references \`town\`, which references \`region\`. Historical versions keep their original lookup rows. A changed tuple gets its own row so earlier versions retain their values.
+- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to \`frame.frame_id\`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
+- Keep grain at the observed frame for address, position, and coordinates. Eight distinct \`site_no\` values map to more than one \`inventory_site_no\`. The reverse has 95 collisions. Even the pair groups several distinct coordinates and addresses. Treating either identifier or the pair as the key for physical location would discard data.
+- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.
+
+### Version and write rules
+
+| Incoming row | Result |
+| --- | --- |
+| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
+| Strictly older source \`modified_date\` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
+| Equal or newer source \`modified_date\` | Set the old row's \`is_current\` to false and its \`valid_to\` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with \`valid_from\` set to that same instant. |
+
+Use \`timestamptz\` for validity. The source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values for comparison. Version intervals are half-open, \`[valid_from, valid_to)\`, with \`valid_to\` null on a current version. A check constraint ties \`is_current\` to whether \`valid_to\` is null and requires a positive closed interval. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.
+
+The operation that accepts a row must create or lock the stable frame row before comparing timestamps. Close and append together in one transaction. Assign the transition instant after acquiring the lock, and make it strictly later than the previous start, including two accepted rows in the same transaction. A partial unique index alone cannot decide whether an upload is stale. Equal-timestamp uploads intentionally append history, including an exact replay. The initial file has one snapshot per frame, so its source timestamps cannot reconstruct earlier revisions. Preserve the last accepted source timestamp when the future UI edit workflow writes a new version.
+
+## Goals and scope
+
+- Deliver a versioned PostgreSQL Flyway migration and wire Spring Boot to apply it during database-backed startup. Reuse the PostgreSQL service and configure startup to wait for readiness. Verify the migration history on first start and restart. The custom \`/api/health\` response alone cannot verify that the migration ran. [Spring Boot database initialization](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-initialization.html) [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
+- Leave CSV parsing, upload endpoints, manual edit endpoints, and history views for their feature work. Keep an ordinary Spring context smoke test usable and verify PostgreSQL-specific DDL on PostgreSQL.
+
+## Alternatives weighed
+
+- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
+- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
+- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.
+
+## Key decisions and implementation staging
+
+The comparison rule and replay behavior are confirmed. Start by creating the referenced tables and their keys, then the version and child tables. Add the current-version index, history index, and validity checks. Wire Flyway into Spring Boot, verify the DDL and a restart on PostgreSQL, and check that every one of the 45 CSV fields has a documented destination or derivation.
+
+The remaining decision is where to enforce the stale-row and close-and-append operation. A SQL write routine would enforce it as part of this migration and can be tested before an importer exists. A later Spring transaction would keep application write rules with the upload and edit workflows, while this migration would provide the structural constraints and indexes.
*** End Patch`));

Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | `frame_version_external_reference` rows keyed by `(version_id, reference_type)`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
| `linked_frame_ids` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered `frame_version_link` rows keyed by `(version_id, position)`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |

### Relational boundaries

- `frame_version` has its own primary key and foreign keys to `frame`, `postcode`, and `frame_format`. `postcode` references `town`, which references `region`. Historical versions keep their original lookup rows. A changed tuple gets its own row so earlier versions retain their values.
- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to `frame.frame_id`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
- Keep grain at the observed frame for address, position, and coordinates. Eight distinct `site_no` values map to more than one `inventory_site_no`. The reverse has 95 collisions. Even the pair groups several distinct coordinates and addresses. Treating either identifier or the pair as the key for physical location would discard data.
- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.

### Version and write rules

| Incoming row | Result |
| --- | --- |
| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
| Strictly older source `modified_date` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
| Equal or newer source `modified_date` | Set the old row's `is_current` to false and its `valid_to` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with `valid_from` set to that same instant. |

Use `timestamptz` for validity. The source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values for comparison. Version intervals are half-open, `[valid_from, valid_to)`, with `valid_to` null on a current version. A check constraint ties `is_current` to whether `valid_to` is null and requires a positive closed interval. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.

The operation that accepts a row must create or lock the stable frame row before comparing timestamps. Close and append together in one transaction. Assign the transition instant after acquiring the lock, and make it strictly later than the previous start, including two accepted rows in the same transaction. A partial unique index alone cannot decide whether an upload is stale. Equal-timestamp uploads intentionally append history, including an exact replay. The initial file has one snapshot per frame, so its source timestamps cannot reconstruct earlier revisions. Preserve the last accepted source timestamp when the future UI edit workflow writes a new version.

## Goals and scope

- Deliver a versioned PostgreSQL Flyway migration and wire Spring Boot to apply it during database-backed startup. Reuse the PostgreSQL service and configure startup to wait for readiness. Verify the migration history on first start and restart. The custom `/api/health` response alone cannot verify that the migration ran. [Spring Boot database initialization](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-initialization.html) [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- Leave CSV parsing, upload endpoints, manual edit endpoints, and history views for their feature work. Keep an ordinary Spring context smoke test usable and verify PostgreSQL-specific DDL on PostgreSQL.

## Alternatives weighed

- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.

## Key decisions and implementation staging

The comparison rule and replay behavior are confirmed. Start by creating the referenced tables and their keys, then the version and child tables. Add the current-version index, history index, and validity checks. Wire Flyway into Spring Boot, verify the DDL and a restart on PostgreSQL, and check that every one of the 45 CSV fields has a documented destination or derivation.

The remaining decision is where to enforce the stale-row and close-and-append operation. A SQL write routine would enforce it as part of this migration and can be tested before an importer exists. A later Spring transaction would keep application write rules with the upload and edit workflows, while this migration would provide the structural constraints and indexes.

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Suggested infrastructure for the Frame Inventory exercise.
#
# This compose file is a starting point, not a requirement. You are free to
# swap any of these services for tooling you prefer (a different database,
# search engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final
# stack still runs end-to-end with a single command.
#
# If you do choose to use the services provided here, pick ONE of the two

services:
  backend:
    build:
      context: ./src/backend
    container_name: frame-inventory-backend
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: docker
    depends_on:
      - postgres
      - opensearch
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  frontend:
    build:
      context: ./src/frontend
    container_name: frame-inventory-frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      BACKEND_URL: http://backend:8080
    volumes:
      - ./src/frontend/src:/app/src
      - ./src/frontend/public:/app/public
    depends_on:
      - backend
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18.6
    container_name: frame-inventory-postgres
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: frames
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

    image: opensearchproject/opensearch:2.18.0
    container_name: frame-inventory-opensearch
    environment:
      cluster.name: frame-inventory-cluster
      node.name: opensearch
      discovery.type: single-node
      bootstrap.memory_lock: "true"
      OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS: "-Xms512m -Xmx512m"
      DISABLE_SECURITY_PLUGIN: "true"
      DISABLE_INSTALL_DEMO_CONFIG: "true"
    ulimits:
      memlock:
        soft: -1
        hard: -1
      nofile:
        soft: 65536
        hard: 65536
    ports:
      - "9200:9200"
      - "9600:9600"
    volumes:
      - opensearch-data:/usr/share/opensearch/data
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

    container_name: frame-inventory-opensearch-dashboards

      DISABLE_SECURITY_DASHBOARDS_PLUGIN: "true"
    depends_on:
      - opensearch
    networks:
      - frame-inventory

volumes:
  postgres-data:
  opensearch-data:

networks:
  frame-inventory:
    driver: bridge

L18: ## 11.8. Partial Indexes 【33†#】
L19: 
L20: A partial index is an index built over a subset of a table; the subset is defined by a conditional expression (called the predicate of the partial index). The index contains entries only for those table rows that satisfy the predicate. Partial indexes are a specialized feature, but there are several situations in which they are useful.
L21: One major reason for using a partial index is to avoid indexing common values. Since a query searching for a common value (one that accounts for more than a few percent of all the table rows) will not use the index anyway, there is no point in keeping those rows in the index at all. This reduces the size of the index, which will speed up those queries that do use the index. It will also speed up many table update operations because the index does not need to be updated in all cases.
L22: 【34†Example 11.1】 shows a possible application of this idea.
L23: Example 11.1. Setting up a Partial Index to Exclude Common Values
L24: 
L25: Suppose you are storing web server access logs in a database. Most accesses originate from the IP address range of your organization but some are from elsewhere (say, employees on dial-up connections). If your searches by IP are primarily for outside accesses, you probably do not need to index the IP range that corresponds to your organization's subnet.
L26: Assume a table like this:
L27: 
L28:     CREATE TABLE access_log (
L29:         url varchar,
L30:         client_ip inet,
L31:         ...
L32:     );
L33: 
L34: 
L35: To create a partial index that suits our example, use a command such as this:
L36: 
L37:     CREATE INDEX access_log_client_ip_ix ON access_log (client_ip)
L38:     WHERE NOT (client_ip > inet '192.168.100.0' AND
L39:                client_ip < inet '192.168.100.255');
L40: A typical query that can use this index would be:
L41: 
L42:     SELECT *
L43:     FROM access_log
L44:     WHERE url = '/index.html' AND client_ip = inet '212.78.10.32';
L45: 
L46: 
L47: Here the query's IP address is covered by the partial index. The following query cannot use the partial index, as it uses an IP address that is excluded from the index:
L48: 
L49:     SELECT *
L50:     FROM access_log
L51:     WHERE url = '/index.html' AND client_ip = inet '192.168.100.23';
L52: Observe that this kind of partial index requires that the common values be predetermined, so such partial indexes are best used for data distributions that do not change. Such indexes can be recreated occasionally to adjust for new data distributions, but this adds maintenance effort.
L53: Another possible use for a partial index is to exclude values from the index that the typical query workload is not interested in; this is shown in 【35†Example 11.2】. This results in the same advantages as listed above, but it prevents the “uninteresting” values from being accessed via that index, even if an index scan might be profitable in that case. Obviously, setting up partial indexes for this kind of scenario will require a lot of care and experimentation.
L54: Example 11.2. Setting up a Partial Index to Exclude Uninteresting Values
L55: 
L56: If you have a table that contains both billed and unbilled orders, where the unbilled orders take up a small fraction of the total table and yet those are the most-accessed rows, you can improve performance by creating an index on just the unbilled rows. The command to create the index would look like this:
L57: 
L58:     CREATE INDEX orders_unbilled_index ON orders (order_nr)
L59:         WHERE billed is not true;
L60: A possible query to use this index would be:
L61: 
L62:     SELECT * FROM orders WHERE billed is not true AND order_nr < 10000;
L63: 
L64: 
L65: However, the index can also be used in queries that do not involve `order_nr` at all, e.g.:
L66: 
L67:     SELECT * FROM orders WHERE billed is not true AND amount > 5000.00;
L68: This is not as efficient as a partial index on the `amount` column would be, since the system has to scan the entire index. Yet, if there are relatively few unbilled orders, using this partial index just to find the unbilled orders could be a win.
L69: 
L70: Note that this query cannot use this index:
L71: 
L72:     SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_nr = 3501;
L73: 
L74: 
L75: The order 3501 might be among the billed or unbilled orders.
L76: 【35†Example 11.2】 also illustrates that the indexed column and the column used in the predicate do not need to match. PostgreSQL supports partial indexes with arbitrary predicates, so long as only columns of the table being indexed are involved. However, keep in mind that the predicate must match the conditions used in the queries that are supposed to benefit from the index.
L77: To be precise, a partial index can be used in a query only if the system can recognize that the `WHERE` condition of the query mathematically implies the predicate of the index. PostgreSQL does not have a sophisticated theorem prover that can recognize mathematically equivalent expressions that are written in different forms.
L78: (Not only is such a general theorem prover extremely difficult to create, it would probably be too slow to be of any real use.) The system can recognize simple inequality implications, for example “x < 1” implies “x < 2”; otherwise the predicate condition must exactly match part of the query's `WHERE` condition or the index will not be recognized as usable. Matching takes place at query planning time, not at run time. As a result, parameterized query clauses do not work with a partial index.
L79: For example a prepared query with a parameter might specify “x < ?” which will never imply “x < 2” for all possible values of the parameter.
L80: A third possible use for partial indexes does not require the index to be used in queries at all. The idea here is to create a unique index over a subset of a table, as in 【36†Example 11.3】. This enforces uniqueness among the rows that satisfy the index predicate, without constraining those that do not.
L81: 
L82: Example 11.3. Setting up a Partial Unique Index
L83: Suppose that we have a table describing test outcomes. We wish to ensure that there is only one “successful” entry for a given subject and target combination, but there might be any number of “unsuccessful” entries. Here is one way to do it:
L84: 
L85:     CREATE TABLE tests (
L86:         subject text,
L87:         target text,
L88:         success boolean,
L89:         ...
L90:     );
L91: 
L92:     CREATE UNIQUE INDEX tests_success_constraint ON tests (subject, target)
L93:         WHERE success;
L94: This is a particularly efficient approach when there are few successful tests and many unsuccessful ones. It is also possible to allow only one null in a column by creating a unique partial index with an `IS NULL` restriction.

Page last updated 12 November 2026

  * Verified Versions: 9.2, 18

## Supported Versions and Support Levels

  * For information regarding the supported version and support levels available, please see Supported Databases for Flyway

## Driver

Item  | Details
--- | ---
Item  | Details

URL format  | `jdbc:postgresql://host:port/database`

Maven Central coordinates  | `org.postgresql:postgresql`
Supported versions  | `9.3-1104-jdbc4` and later

PostgreSQL support is a separate dependency for Flyway and will need to be added to your Java project to access these features. PostgreSQL is found within the `flyway-database-postgresql` plugin module.

The schema separates stable frame identities from version history, normalizes shared location and format data, and enforces at most one current version per frame.

The [schema brief](/Users/alexcallow/Sites/frame-inventory-exercise-main/concepts_brief.md) maps all 45 CSV fields and records the contract for the future shared `@Transactional` service. That service will enforce stale-row rejection and atomic close-and-append across CSV upload, create, and edit.

# Frame inventory schema and version history

- **Author** Alex Callow
- **Date** 2026-11-26

## Overview

Use PostgreSQL to store frames and their accepted versions. Each `frame_id` identifies one frame through successive uploads. An incoming row whose `modified_date` is strictly older than the current row is ignored. An equal or newer value closes the previous version and opens the next version at the same import instant.

The supplied extract has 1,000 rows, 1,000 distinct frame IDs, and 45 fields. The migration will create the schema on Spring Boot startup. The exercise calls for a user-driven CSV upload, so the migration will start with empty inventory tables. [CSV](./data/inventory_frame.csv) [Exercise requirements](./INSTRUCTIONS.md#L52-L64)

## Analysis

### Raw field mapping

CSV values arrive as text. The types below describe how to parse them for PostgreSQL. A blank optional value becomes SQL `NULL`. Observed null counts and value sets describe this extract.

| CSV fields | Observed representation | Proposed PostgreSQL mapping |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame_id` | Ten decimal digits, unique and populated in all rows | `frame.frame_id text` primary key. The prototype also uses alphanumeric frame IDs. |
| `created_date`, `modified_date` | Date and time to seconds, without offsets | `frame_version` source timestamps, `timestamp without time zone`. |
| `country_code`, `region`, `town` | Codes and names. One country, 12 regions, 172 towns | Country code and region name form the region's natural key. Town name is scoped to a region. Each table also has a generated primary key. |
| `postcode` | UK postcode with a space, 484 distinct | `postcode` row keyed by generated ID, unique on `(town_id, postcode)`. |
| `postcode_area`, `postcode_district`, `postcode_sector`, `postcode_unit` | Text fragments, some containing letters | Derive from the postcode. The four fragments reconstruct it exactly in all 1,000 rows. |
| `longitude`, `latitude` | Signed decimal degrees | Exact `numeric` columns on `frame_version`, with valid coordinate ranges. |
| `location` | `POINT (latitude longitude)` text | Derive from the scalar coordinates if an export requires the legacy format. All 1,000 rows contain the same pair in this order. |
| `site_no`, `inventory_site_no`, `panel_number` | Identifiers. Site and panel numbers can contain leading zeros | Independent `text` fields on `frame_version`. |
| `location_id` | Identifier, 13 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. In 67 rows the populated value differs from the normalized postcode. |
| `environment`, `address`, `station`, `airport` | Text. Station has 593 blanks and airport has 887 | `text` on `frame_version`, with the optional site names nullable. |
| `type_classic_digital`, `format`, `size_group_code` | Codes. Nine distinct combinations | `frame_format` row keyed by generated ID, unique on the three codes. Codes stay as text, including size groups such as `006`. |
| `size_code`, `aspect_ratio_code`, `t_size` | Codes and labels. `t_size` has 57 blanks | `text` columns on `frame_version`. |
| `pixel_height`, `pixel_width` | Positive integers, 28 blanks in each column | Nullable `integer` dimensions on `frame_version`. |
| `illumination_type_id`, `number_of_slots`, `distance_to_closest_school` | Integer code and counts or distances | `integer` on `frame_version`. The proposed distance unit is metres, consistent with the prototype. |
| `status`, `status_reason` | Text. Every row is `LIVE` and all reasons are blank | Status and nullable reason on `frame_version`. |
| `impact_weight` | Decimal, six blanks | Nullable exact `numeric` on `frame_version`. |
| `premium` | `0` or `1` | `boolean` on `frame_version`. |
| `production_rate_card`, `production_rate_card_legacy` | Both columns are blank throughout | Separate nullable `text` fields until the source contract establishes how they relate. |
| `pricing_grade` | Text, 869 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. |
| `price_entity_id`, `broadsign_display_unit_id`, `broadsign_frame_id`, `broadsign_domain_id` | Opaque codes. Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | `frame_version_external_reference` rows keyed by `(version_id, reference_type)`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
| `linked_frame_ids` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered `frame_version_link` rows keyed by `(version_id, position)`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |

### Relational boundaries

- `frame_version` has its own primary key and foreign keys to `frame`, `postcode`, and `frame_format`. `postcode` references `town`, which references `region`. Historical versions keep their original lookup rows. A changed tuple gets its own row so earlier versions retain their values.
- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to `frame.frame_id`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
- Keep grain at the observed frame for address, position, and coordinates. Eight distinct `site_no` values map to more than one `inventory_site_no`. The reverse has 95 collisions. Even the pair groups several distinct coordinates and addresses. Treating either identifier or the pair as the key for physical location would discard data.
- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.

### Version and write rules

| Incoming row | Result |
| --- | --- |
| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
| Strictly older source `modified_date` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
| Equal or newer source `modified_date` | Set the old row's `is_current` to false and its `valid_to` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with `valid_from` set to that same instant. |

Use `timestamptz` for validity. The source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values for comparison. Version intervals are half-open, `[valid_from, valid_to)`, with `valid_to` null on a current version. A check constraint ties `is_current` to whether `valid_to` is null and requires a positive closed interval. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.

The operation that accepts a row must create or lock the stable frame row before comparing timestamps. Close and append together in one transaction. Assign the transition instant after acquiring the lock, and make it strictly later than the previous start, including two accepted rows in the same transaction. A partial unique index alone cannot decide whether an upload is stale. Equal-timestamp uploads intentionally append history, including an exact replay. The initial file has one snapshot per frame, so its source timestamps cannot reconstruct earlier revisions. Preserve the last accepted source timestamp when the future UI edit workflow writes a new version.

## Goals and scope

- Deliver a versioned PostgreSQL Flyway migration and wire Spring Boot to apply it during database-backed startup. Reuse the PostgreSQL service and configure startup to wait for readiness. Verify the migration history on first start and restart. The custom `/api/health` response alone cannot verify that the migration ran. [Spring Boot database initialization](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-initialization.html) [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- Leave CSV parsing, upload endpoints, manual edit endpoints, and history views for their feature work. Keep an ordinary Spring context smoke test usable and verify PostgreSQL-specific DDL on PostgreSQL.

## Alternatives weighed

- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.

## Key decisions and implementation staging

The comparison rule and replay behavior are confirmed. Start by creating the referenced tables and their keys, then the version and child tables. Add the current-version index, history index, and validity checks. Wire Flyway into Spring Boot, verify the DDL and a restart on PostgreSQL, and check that every one of the 45 CSV fields has a documented destination or derivation.

The migration owns the schema, keys, validity checks, and indexes. The future
CSV upload, create, and edit paths will call a shared Spring
`@Transactional` service for the stable-row lock and close-and-append
operation. The CSV path supplies `source_modified_at` for the stale check.
Manual edits carry forward the previous source timestamp. Manual creation can
start with null source timestamps.

# Frame inventory schema and version history

- **Author** Alex Callow
- **Date** 2026-11-26

## Overview

Use PostgreSQL to store frames and their accepted versions. Each `frame_id` identifies one frame through successive uploads. An incoming row whose `modified_date` is strictly older than the current row is ignored. An equal or newer value closes the previous version and opens the next version at the same import instant.

The supplied extract has 1,000 rows, 1,000 distinct frame IDs, and 45 fields. The migration will create the schema on Spring Boot startup. The exercise calls for a user-driven CSV upload, so the migration will start with empty inventory tables. [CSV](./data/inventory_frame.csv) [Exercise requirements](./INSTRUCTIONS.md#L52-L64)

## Analysis

### Raw field mapping

CSV values arrive as text. The types below describe how to parse them for PostgreSQL. A blank optional value becomes SQL `NULL`. Observed null counts and value sets describe this extract.

| CSV fields | Observed representation | Proposed PostgreSQL mapping |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `frame_id` | Ten decimal digits, unique and populated in all rows | `frame.frame_id text` primary key. The prototype also uses alphanumeric frame IDs. |
| `created_date`, `modified_date` | Date and time to seconds, without offsets | `frame_version` source timestamps, `timestamp without time zone`. |
| `country_code`, `region`, `town` | Codes and names. One country, 12 regions, 172 towns | Country code and region name form the region's natural key. Town name is scoped to a region. Each table also has a generated primary key. |
| `postcode` | UK postcode with a space, 484 distinct | `postcode` row keyed by generated ID, unique on `(town_id, postcode)`. |
| `postcode_area`, `postcode_district`, `postcode_sector`, `postcode_unit` | Text fragments, some containing letters | Derive from the postcode. The four fragments reconstruct it exactly in all 1,000 rows. |
| `longitude`, `latitude` | Signed decimal degrees | Exact `numeric` columns on `frame_version`, with valid coordinate ranges. |
| `location` | `POINT (latitude longitude)` text | Derive from the scalar coordinates if an export requires the legacy format. All 1,000 rows contain the same pair in this order. |
| `site_no`, `inventory_site_no`, `panel_number` | Identifiers. Site and panel numbers can contain leading zeros | Independent `text` fields on `frame_version`. |
| `location_id` | Identifier, 13 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. In 67 rows the populated value differs from the normalized postcode. |
| `environment`, `address`, `station`, `airport` | Text. Station has 593 blanks and airport has 887 | `text` on `frame_version`, with the optional site names nullable. |
| `type_classic_digital`, `format`, `size_group_code` | Codes. Nine distinct combinations | `frame_format` row keyed by generated ID, unique on the three codes. Codes stay as text, including size groups such as `006`. |
| `size_code`, `aspect_ratio_code`, `t_size` | Codes and labels. `t_size` has 57 blanks | `text` columns on `frame_version`. |
| `pixel_height`, `pixel_width` | Positive integers, 28 blanks in each column | Nullable `integer` dimensions on `frame_version`. |
| `illumination_type_id`, `number_of_slots`, `distance_to_closest_school` | Integer code and counts or distances | `integer` on `frame_version`. The proposed distance unit is metres, consistent with the prototype. |
| `status`, `status_reason` | Text. Every row is `LIVE` and all reasons are blank | Status and nullable reason on `frame_version`. |
| `impact_weight` | Decimal, six blanks | Nullable exact `numeric` on `frame_version`. |
| `premium` | `0` or `1` | `boolean` on `frame_version`. |
| `production_rate_card`, `production_rate_card_legacy` | Both columns are blank throughout | Separate nullable `text` fields until the source contract establishes how they relate. |
| `pricing_grade` | Text, 869 blanks | Nullable `text` on `frame_version`. |
| `price_entity_id`, `broadsign_display_unit_id`, `broadsign_frame_id`, `broadsign_domain_id` | Opaque codes. Broadsign fields have 3, 979, and 29 blanks respectively | `frame_version_external_reference` rows keyed by `(version_id, reference_type)`, with identifier values as text. Values can recur across frames. |
| `linked_frame_ids` | Comma-separated IDs, present in four rows | Ordered `frame_version_link` rows keyed by `(version_id, position)`, with each target ID as text. Each supplied list includes its source frame and a peer. |

### Relational boundaries

- `frame_version` has its own primary key and foreign keys to `frame`, `postcode`, and `frame_format`. `postcode` references `town`, which references `region`. Historical versions keep their original lookup rows. A changed tuple gets its own row so earlier versions retain their values.
- External references and linked frame IDs belong to the version that carried them. Both child tables reference that version. Resolve a linked target by joining its source ID to `frame.frame_id`. This lets a partial upload preserve a reference before its target arrives.
- Keep grain at the observed frame for address, position, and coordinates. Eight distinct `site_no` values map to more than one `inventory_site_no`. The reverse has 95 collisions. Even the pair groups several distinct coordinates and addresses. Treating either identifier or the pair as the key for physical location would discard data.
- Store format and size-group codes independently in the format tuple. Their values line up one-to-one in this extract. A wider export may contain combinations absent here. Status, technology, and slot count also vary in the intended product even though each is uniform in this sample.

### Version and write rules

| Incoming row | Result |
| --- | --- |
| First row for a frame | Insert the stable frame and its first current version. |
| Strictly older source `modified_date` | Leave the current row, links, and history as they were. |
| Equal or newer source `modified_date` | Set the old row's `is_current` to false and its `valid_to` to the transition instant. Insert a current version with `valid_from` set to that same instant. |

Use `timestamptz` for validity. The source timestamps retain their original wall-clock values for comparison. Version intervals are half-open, `[valid_from, valid_to)`, with `valid_to` null on a current version. A check constraint ties `is_current` to whether `valid_to` is null and requires a positive closed interval. A partial unique index enforces at most one current version per frame.

The operation that accepts a row must create or lock the stable frame row before comparing timestamps. Close and append together in one transaction. Assign the transition instant after acquiring the lock, and make it strictly later than the previous start, including two accepted rows in the same transaction. A partial unique index alone cannot decide whether an upload is stale. Equal-timestamp uploads intentionally append history, including an exact replay. The initial file has one snapshot per frame, so its source timestamps cannot reconstruct earlier revisions. Preserve the last accepted source timestamp when the future UI edit workflow writes a new version.

## Goals and scope

- Deliver a versioned PostgreSQL Flyway migration and wire Spring Boot to apply it during database-backed startup. Reuse the PostgreSQL service and configure startup to wait for readiness. Verify the migration history on first start and restart. The custom `/api/health` response alone cannot verify that the migration ran. [Spring Boot database initialization](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/data-initialization.html) [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/ddl-constraints.html)
- Leave CSV parsing, upload endpoints, manual edit endpoints, and history views for their feature work. Keep an ordinary Spring context smoke test usable and verify PostgreSQL-specific DDL on PostgreSQL.

## Alternatives weighed

- One wide mutable row has a simple current read and loses revisions. A second mutable current table would duplicate the version data and require another write on each transition. Index the current versions in the history table.
- One table per category code would add joins and introduce catalog rules that the extract cannot establish. Share the repeated region, town, postcode, and format tuples and keep frame-specific values with each historical version.
- A foreign key from each linked target to an existing frame gives immediate referential integrity and forces partial uploads to wait for every target. Preserve each source target identifier and enforce the owner foreign key. An unresolved target can join to its frame once that frame arrives.

## Key decisions and implementation staging

The comparison rule and replay behavior are confirmed. Start by creating the referenced tables and their keys, then the version and child tables. Add the current-version index, history index, and validity checks. Wire Flyway into Spring Boot, verify the DDL and a restart on PostgreSQL, and check that every one of the 45 CSV fields has a documented destination or derivation.

The migration owns the schema, keys, validity checks, and indexes. The future
CSV upload, create, and edit paths will call a shared Spring
`@Transactional` service for the stable-row lock and close-and-append
operation. The CSV path supplies `source_modified_at` for the stale check.
Manual edits carry forward the previous source timestamp. Manual creation can
start with null source timestamps.
